projects.title: Keyboard-first Web Calculator

projects.story: This began as a small calculator, then percentages, keyboard shortcuts, history, memory, and JavaScript arithmetic made it less small. I pair-programmed it with Claude Code and kept testing edge cases behind the simple interface. The percent button needed more decisions than I expected.
capabilities: Basic operations with operator precedence and nested parentheses
Scientific actions: square, square root, reciprocal, sign toggle, percent
50-item history with timestamps and click-to-reuse results
Memory controls: MC, MR, M+, M-
Light/dark theme with system preference detection
Keyboard navigation and ARIA labels for calculator controls
Decimal handling for common floating-point cases such as 0.1 + 0.2

projects.title: Screenshot Accessibility Triage
projects.tagline: A screenshot triage tool that flags possible accessibility problems and explains how to check each one. It is not an audit.
projects.story: I built this for the awkward moment when I had only a screenshot but still wanted to start an accessibility review. It flags possible contrast, focus, and labelling issues, gives each one a confidence rating, and suggests a manual check. It can help with triage, but it cannot inspect source code or replace manual testing and accessibility tools.
capabilities: Accepts drag-and-drop PNG and JPG screenshots, then runs heuristic checks
Switches between web UI and Windows desktop UI targets
Flags visual cues that may indicate contrast, focus, icon-only button, keyboard, or focus-order issues
Lists each finding with a confidence rating and a manual verification step
Exports findings as JSON or bug-report text
Runs as an Electron desktop app with a Vite renderer

projects.title: Design Relay
projects.tagline: A work-in-progress tool for comparing a selected Figma design with Azure DevOps changes and drafting a report for human review.
projects.problem: The first version tried to handle reviews, Figma search, scenario generation, discovery, and settings at once. That buried its main job: connect a design to a code change, compare them, and show the basis for the report.
projects.portfolio_signal: I cut the proposed flow to four steps: Connect, Discover, Analyze, and Report. The adapters still do the technical work, but a designer or engineer makes the final judgement.
evidence: A CLI and MCP entry point can gather Azure DevOps pull-request context for a review run.
The tool keeps Figma and repository inputs separate instead of merging them into one model prompt.
Dry-run mode shows the output before anything is posted to the pull request.
The refactor brief cuts the first version down to one path.
limitations: The planned refactor does not yet include token onboarding, workspace scanning, or secure credential storage.
Automatic Figma-to-repository matching is currently a naming heuristic, not a reliable relationship model.
Visual comparison depends on the selected frame, implementation state, and viewport.
A person still needs to review the findings before anything is posted.
projects.learning: Renaming the project from Design Review Bot to Design Relay clarified the job: carry design and code context into one report, then leave the decision to people.
projects.story:
I built the first version to reduce the setup work at the start of an Azure DevOps design review. It gathered pull-request context, read Figma data, ran a vision pass, and drafted a review. Then I added review, discovery, Figma search, scenario generation, and settings until no task felt primary.

The refactor narrows the product to four steps: connect Figma and Azure DevOps, find likely file-to-repository matches, analyse one pair, and return a report that shows what was compared. The CLI and MCP integrations are further along than this flow, so the project remains a work in progress.

It should not act as an automated design authority. The intended first pass flags possible differences in spacing, type, colour, components, and layout, explains what it compared, and leaves the final call to the designer and engineer.
capabilities: Starts an Azure DevOps pull-request review from the CLI or MCP server
Accepts a pull-request ID and reads repository, project, and organisation values from overrides or Azure DevOps pipeline environment variables
Pulls PR context and compares code changes with Figma-derived design info
Exposes an MCP server entrypoint for agent-based usage
Supports dry-run output instead of posting back to the PR
projects.run_cmd: npm install && npm run build && npm run start:mcp

projects.title: System Messages
projects.tagline: A field guide to confirmations, boundaries, access notices, and other chat messages that should not sound like the assistant.
projects.problem: Designing system notices one at a time leads to inconsistent treatment as a chat product grows. Confirmations, session boundaries, access notices, errors, and ordinary UI changes begin to look and sound alike.
projects.portfolio_signal: I kept the interface quiet so the classification and rules carry the page. It groups system messages into four categories and documents when to use each one, how it behaves, and how to write it.
evidence: Four categories cover action acknowledgements, session lifecycle markers, context boundaries, and conversation-wide access notices.
A decision tree distinguishes system messages from assistant output, application errors, and UI state changes.
Each category documents anatomy, placement, persistence, timing, interaction, and content rules.
The public prototype includes a sidebar, table of contents, examples, and a single-page reading path.
limitations: The site documents the classification and rules; it has no authoring workflow or component playground.
Examples omit internal product scenarios, policy, and visual tokens.
The taxonomy still needs broader scenario testing to expose ambiguous or overlapping cases.
The prototype has no search, contribution model, version history, or automated documentation tests.
projects.learning: The rule I kept returning to was simple. If a state change adds no information, leave it in the interface instead of announcing it in the conversation.
projects.story:
System messages record facts inside a chat: an action finished, a session ended, a visibility rule starts here, or the whole conversation has a special access condition. They belong to neither the user nor the assistant, but they affect how someone reads the timeline.

I grouped them into four categories and added a decision tree for a harder question: when should there be no system message at all? Assistant output, service errors, and ordinary interface changes need different treatment. Narrating every state change adds noise.

The prototype is a field guide, not an app. One page documents message parts, placement, persistence, timing, interaction, and writing rules. It also gives a team a shared vocabulary and a way to reject messages that add no information.
capabilities: Four categories for system messages
Decision tree for choosing between a system message, assistant output, application error, or UI state
One-page guide with a sidebar and table of contents
Guidance on message parts, content, placement, persistence, timing, and interaction
Rules for distinguishing chat output, message bars, and UI state changes

projects.title: Agent Canvas
projects.tagline: A Figma-like canvas for mapping an agent's steps, decisions, responses, and quality criteria.
projects.problem: Agent behaviour is often split across prompts, configuration, and orchestration code. That makes product decisions hard to see, critique, or hand off.
projects.portfolio_signal: I wanted agent behaviour to be something a team could inspect together. The prototype maps steps, decisions, responses, and weighted quality criteria on one canvas.
evidence: Three sample scenarios model onboarding, file analysis, and error recovery as connected five-step flows.
The canvas uses four step types: trigger, action, decision, and response.
Quality criteria carry must, should, and nice-to-have weights rather than sitting in a separate checklist.
Preview mode replays a simulated conversation and highlights its active canvas node.
limitations: The preview currently replays one hard-coded scenario rather than compiling the flow being edited.
Edits live only in local component state; refresh the page and they are gone.
Dragging, adding steps, and some toolbar controls appear in the interface but do not work yet.
There is no agent backend, persistence layer, automated test suite, or deployment yet.
projects.learning: The prototype exposed a more immediate gap than persistence: Preview does not compile the flow being edited. Until it does, the canvas and conversation are linked demonstrations, not one authoring tool.
projects.story:
We could draw a user flow, write a prompt, or make a prototype, but none put an agent's turn-by-turn behaviour in one place. I sketched a node-based canvas that borrows from Figma without treating conversation as a simple flowchart.

Each scenario uses typed steps. Selecting one opens its instruction, output, and quality criteria in the inspector. Preview replays a short simulated conversation and highlights the active message and canvas node together.

The interface is ahead of the implementation. The drag handles do not work, edits disappear on refresh, and the preview is hard-coded. I built enough interaction to ask whether a designer, PM, and engineer could discuss the same behaviour on the canvas.
capabilities: Switch between editable flow and conversation preview modes
Browse three sample agent scenarios
Inspect typed trigger, action, decision, and response steps
Edit step instructions and toggle weighted quality criteria
Replay a simulated conversation with active-step highlighting
Pan and zoom around the canvas

projects.title: Behavior Diff
projects.tagline: A word-level before-and-after view of one prompt, constraint, or input change.
projects.problem: A small change to a prompt, policy, or context can produce a very different response. Two full outputs side by side make those differences hard to locate.
projects.portfolio_signal: The prototype allows one changed variable per scenario, so each comparison stays tied to a specific prompt, constraint, or input edit.
evidence: Three fixtures each change one thing: the response requirements, a VIP constraint, or the customer's message.
A custom longest-common-subsequence engine computes word-level additions, removals, and unchanged spans.
Split and unified views share one diff result, with line alignment and empty rows keeping comparisons legible.
The interface also shows change counts, the exact configuration difference, and a simulated rerun state.
limitations: The outputs are authored fixtures; the rerun button does not call a live model.
All three scenarios use customer support, so the prototype has not been tried across other domains.
Configuration is visible but not editable, so new experiments still require code changes.
There is no backend, persistence, automated test suite, or committed deployment.
projects.learning: If I change three things and compare two outputs, I learn almost nothing. Each scenario therefore names its one changed variable before showing the red-and-green diff.
projects.story:
Agent changes can look small in configuration and much larger in the response. I wanted a code-style diff that marks added, removed, and unchanged wording instead of reducing the comparison to a better-or-worse score.

The prototype has three controlled scenarios. One changes the response requirements, one adds a VIP constraint, and one changes the incoming message. A custom word-level diff feeds both split and unified views, so both modes show the same comparison.

The rerun is simulated and the outputs are authored fixtures. That let me work on the comparison interface before building live model runs. The views have not yet been tested with variable, non-deterministic output.
capabilities: Switch between three one-variable scenarios
Compare outputs in split or unified views
Inspect word-level additions, removals, and unchanged text
Read a summary of additions, removals, and unchanged text
See the exact configuration, constraint, or input delta
Replay a simulated before-and-after run

projects.title: Conversation Pattern Library
projects.tagline: A searchable library of six conversation patterns, with guidance, anatomy, and replayable examples.
projects.problem: Teams often solve the same conversation problems inside separate mockups: clarifying an ambiguous request, revealing complexity gradually, recovering context, and confirming a risky action. The reasoning rarely travels with the design.
projects.portfolio_signal: The library records repeated conversation decisions together with the situations and limits that determine when each pattern applies. It currently contains six patterns.
evidence: Six authored patterns span clarification, disclosure, error handling, handoff, and confirmation.
Every pattern includes when-to-use guidance, principles, four anatomy steps, a conversation example, and tags.
Search matches names, descriptions, and tags; category filters update the visible library count.
Live Preview, Anatomy, and Guidelines views let the same pattern be read as an example, a structure, or practical advice.
limitations: The library contains six patterns and is not a comprehensive system.
Patterns are static TypeScript data with no authoring, review, or contribution workflow.
There are no deep links to a selected pattern, and browser history does not capture exploration.
Related patterns are mentioned but are not modelled or linked in the interface.
projects.learning: This build documents when each pattern applies and where it stops. It does not yet link patterns that often appear in the same conversation.
projects.story:
I designed the library around a practical task: find a pattern for a specific situation, understand its limits, and follow it across several turns. The chat bubbles come after that.

The library contains six patterns: Clarification Loop, Progressive Disclosure, Graceful Fallback, Escalation to Human, Destructive Action Confirmation, and Context Recovery. They share one data schema, which drives search, category filters, anatomy diagrams, guidelines, and replayable examples.

Six patterns are a starting set, not a full design system, and there is no contribution workflow yet. Related patterns also need links because one conversation may use several.
capabilities: Search patterns by name, description, or tags
Filter across five conversation-design categories
Browse a compact, collapsible pattern index
Switch between Live Preview, Anatomy, and Guidelines
Replay multi-turn examples with agent, user, and system roles
Inspect principles, tags, and when-to-use guidance

projects.title: Figma Redline Bridge
projects.tagline: A local bridge that lets an AI or script draw measurements, specs, and annotation batches inside Figma.
projects.problem: Figma's Plugin API runs inside its sandbox, so an external tool cannot directly draw into the open file. I wanted a local command path that I could inspect, mainly to stop drawing the same spacing arrows by hand.
projects.portfolio_signal: The project combines a Node relay, WebSocket connection, plugin iframe, Figma runtime, and commands for drawing annotations. Most of the work sits in the handoffs between those parts.
evidence: A four-hop command path connects HTTP clients to a Node relay, WebSocket, plugin iframe, and Figma sandbox.
Remote commands cover spacing, dimensions, colour, typography, page creation, and ordered batches.
The server queues commands while Figma is disconnected and exposes connection state through a health endpoint.
The plugin preserves auto-layout by rescaling cloned frames rather than mutating dimensions directly.
limitations: The localhost command endpoint is unauthenticated and should not be exposed beyond a trusted local machine.
Only one active Figma client is supported; a new connection replaces the previous socket.
Batch commands fail when Figma is disconnected instead of joining the normal pending-command queue.
Setup still requires a server process, a plugin build, and a manually loaded Figma development manifest.
There is no automated test suite for the cross-runtime message path.
projects.learning: Drawing a line was straightforward. Moving a command through three runtimes and Figma's sandbox without breaking auto-layout was not. A plain protocol made the route easier to debug.
projects.story:
I began with a narrow test: send a command from an external tool and draw a spacing redline in the open Figma file. Figma's sandbox made that a multi-step route.

The local relay turns an HTTP request into a WebSocket message, passes it through the plugin iframe with postMessage, and calls the Figma API. Replies travel back along the same route. I added commands for spacing, dimensions, colour, typography, page creation, and ordered batches.

The project later expanded into documentation experiments, but the bridge remains the part I care about. It automates repetition without claiming to automate taste. A person chooses what needs an annotation; the tool draws it.
capabilities: Send structured commands from an AI, CLI, or local script into Figma
Draw spacing measurements and dimension labels
Generate colour swatches and typography specification boxes
Create pages and execute ordered command batches
Queue pending commands until the plugin connects
Inspect server and Figma connection state through a health endpoint

projects.title: FlowSense
projects.tagline: A screen-recording review tool that links rubric scores and findings to the frames they came from.
projects.problem: A screenshot cannot show delayed feedback, backtracking, or an error that ends a flow. Reviewing the recording can, but manual findings take time and vary by reviewer.
projects.portfolio_signal: I turned a UX review rubric into an upload, processing, and report flow. Each finding links to a source frame, so a designer can check the cited moment instead of accepting the score alone.
evidence: A seven-category weighted rubric returns a score from 0 to 100 and a pass, warn, or block result.
The processor extracts frames, selects visible interaction changes, and keeps fact extraction separate from rubric scoring.
Reports link issues and recommendations back to source frames, then compare repeat runs for regressions.
The processing path uses signed webhooks, nonce replay checks, managed identity, and atomic SQL claims.
The monorepo includes focused tests, CI checks, shared schemas, and a test harness for agreement and release metrics.
limitations: It depends on configured Azure services and credentials, so it is not a one-click public demo.
Local development bypasses authentication. A deployment must re-enable it.
The repository has benchmark code but no populated, human-labelled holdout set.
If a long recording exceeds the analysis budget, the result can warn but cannot pass.
A designer still has to decide whether the rubric suits the product and whether the cited frames support each finding.
projects.learning: The model runs in two passes. One answers 'What happened?' The second scores those facts against the rubric. That split made the findings easier for me to trace than a single prompt did.
projects.story:
FlowSense began with a question: could a recorded user flow be checked against a consistent rubric without treating the score as objective truth? I wanted a repeatable first pass without hiding uncertainty behind one number.

It grew from a local model experiment into a monorepo with an upload interface, video processor, shared schemas, storage, frame analysis, and reports. The key change was splitting the model work into two passes. One describes observable interaction events; the other scores those events against the rubric.

I added checks around the score. Issues link to frames. Repeat runs show differences. A truncated analysis can warn but cannot pass. The tool still needs a designer to review the findings and the rubric.
capabilities: Upload and process UX screen recordings
Extract frames and select visible interaction changes
Use one vision pass to record interaction facts and another to apply the seven-category rubric
Show a pass, warn, or block result with findings, recommendations, source frames, and differences from a previous run
Navigate from report findings back to source frames
Store runs and media with Azure SQL and Blob Storage
Protect processor calls with signed webhooks and replay checks
Export review reports as PDF
